citation: Rolls, Barbara J., Pearce, Alaina L., (2026) Whole versus Parts 1988 [Dataset]. ScholarSphere.
description: These data are from a study that included two counterbalanced visits and a follow-up discharge session. The counterbalanced condition was whether participants were served the sandwiches as whole units or cut into pieces. Participants included men and women without overweight or obesity who were not dieting. Visits were conducted at approximately 11:30 in the morning. Participants were given visual analog (VAS) scales to rate their hunger, thirst, fullness, desire to eat, and how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption). They were then asked to rate the pleasantness of the taste and their desire to eat a sample of a ham and Swiss cheese sandwich with lettuce and mustard on rye bread. Participants were then presented with either four whole ham and Swiss cheese sandwiches on rye bread (held together with toothpicks) or the same sandwiches cut into nine small squares, each held together with a toothpick. They were also given a 550 g glass of cold water and a timer. They were told to eat as much as they wanted within 20 minutes and to ask for more if they desired. They were not allowed to read, do any work, or socialize during this time. All VAS ratings were repeated after the participants finished eating the sandwiches. Total intake was computed by weight the sandwiches and water before and after the meal.

citation: Rolls, Barbara J., & Pearce, Alaina L. (2026) Sociofeed: Danny's Dinner 1990 [Dataset]. ScholarSphere.
description: These data are from a study that included two counterbalanced visits. The counterbalanced condition was whether participants ate a meal alone or with three other individuals matched on gender and eating restraint. For the group condition, it was randomly assigned whether the other individuals were known friends or strangers. Participants completed the Eating Inventory and were categorized as restrained or unrestrained eaters. Participants included men and women without overweight or obesity who were not dieting. Visits were conducted at dinner. Participants were given visual analog scales (VAS) before and after eating to rate their current mood, arousal state, hunger, thirst, fullness, and how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption). Participants were then presented with a spaghetti meal and water. They were told to eat as much as they wanted within 40 minutes and to ask for more if desired. Total intake was computed by weighing the food and water before and after the meal.
related_publications: Oral Presentation: Shide, David J. & Rolls, Barbara J. (1995) Social Facilitation of Caloric Intake in Humans by Friends, But Not by Strangers. Society for the Study of Ingestive Behavior

citation: Rolls, Barbara J., & Pearce, Alaina L. (2026) Yogurt SSS by Age 1990 [Dataset]. ScholarSphere.
description: The goal of this study was to examine the role of age on sensory-specific satiety. These data are from a study that included two visits. Participants varied in age across four different age groups. At each visit, participants completed visual analog scales (VAS) to report their current state (e.g., hunger, thirst, nausea, fullness, and how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption)) before and after eating. Participants were served two different amounts of yogurt, with the amount served at each visit counterbalanced across participants. Participants were also asked to taste a series of foods and use a VAS to rate pleasantness of food attributes before and after eating the yogurt.
related_publications: Rolls, Barbara J., and Teresa M. McDermott. "Effects of age on sensory-specific satiety." The American journal of clinical nutrition 54, no. 6 (1991): 988-996.

citation: Rolls, Barbara J., & Pearce, Alaina L. (2026) Eating Disorders Studies 1991 [Dataset]. ScholarSphere.
description: These data are from inpatients from the Johns Hopkins Hospital Eating Disorder Unit and control participants from the surrounding community. All participants completed questionnaires, ratings, and a cafeteria meal. All study sessions were completed at lunchtime. Participants were given visual analog scales (VAS) before and after eating the cafeteria meal to rate their current mood, arousal state, hunger, thirst, fullness, and how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption). Participants were then able to choose meal foods from the cafeteria and consumed the meal with a clinician, who also ate. Inpatient participants completed the sessions before and after treatment, while control participants completed the session twice, separated by a few weeks.

description: These data are from inpatients from the Johns Hopkins Hospital Eating Disorder Unit and control participants from the surrounding community. citation: Rolls, Barbara J., & Pearce, Alaina L. (2026) Eating Disorders Studies 1991 [Dataset]. ScholarSphere.
description: These data are from inpatients from the Johns Hopkins Hospital Eating Disorder Unit and control participants from the surrounding community. Participants completed three sessions in counterbalanced order on alternating days of the first week of their hospital admission. During each session, participants received one of three yogurt preloads for lunch: high fat, high carbohydrate, or low fat/low carbohydrate. Participants rated their current state including hunger, fullness, desire to eat, how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption), bloatedness, fear of becoming fat, desire to binge and purge, alertness, guilt, depression, contentment, and nausea before and after the yogurt preload, before and after dinner, and every 60 minutes between the preload and dinner (four times).
related_publications: Rolls BJ, Hetherington MM, Stoner SA, Andersen AE. Effects of preloads of differing energy and macronutrient content on eating behavior in bulimia nervosa. Appetite. 1997 Dec 1;29(3):353-67.

citation: Rolls, Barbara J., & Pearce, Alaina L. (2026) Eating Disorders Studies 1991 [Dataset]. ScholarSphere.
description: These data are from inpatients from the Johns Hopkins Hospital Eating Disorder Unit and control participants from the surrounding community. Participants completed two sessions in counterbalanced order,with at least one non-test day between sessions, during the first week after admission to the hospital. Participants completed a food diary followed by rating their hunger, thirst, desire to eat, fullness, prospective consumption (i.e. how much they thought they could eat), bloatedness, fear of fatness, desire to binge, desire to purge, alertness, guilt, depression, contentedness, and nausea using 100 mm visual analog scales (VAS). Participants were then served dinner, which was eaten alone. After dinner, participants completed the same VAS ratings. In the deprivation condition, participants fasted starting at 10:00 p.m. the night prior to the session (or after dinner at 6:00 p.m. for inpatient participants). The non-deprivation condition did not restrict prior food intake. The meals were also video recorded and coded for eating behaviors.
related_publications: Hetherington MM, Stoner SA, Andersen AE, Rolls BJ. Effects of acute food deprivation on eating behavior in eating disorders. International Journal of Eating Disorders. 2000 Nov;28(3):272-83.

description: These data are from inpatients from the Johns Hopkins Hospital Eating Disorder Unit and control participants from the surrounding community. citation: Rolls, Barbara J., & Pearce, Alaina L. (2026) Eating Disorders Studies 1991 [Dataset]. ScholarSphere.
description: These data are from inpatients from the Johns Hopkins Hospital Eating Disorder Unit and control participants from the surrounding community. Participants completed three sessions in counterbalanced order on alternating days of the first week of their hospital admission. During each session, participants received one of three condition preloads for lunch: high calorie salad preload, low calorie salad preload, or no preload. Participants rated their current state including hunger, fullness, desire to eat, how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption), bloatedness, fear of becoming fat, desire to binge and purge, alertness, guilt, depression, contentment, and nausea before and after the yogurt preload, and before and after lunch (four times). citation: Rolls, Barbara J., Pearce, Alaina L., (2026) IV versus IG Preload Study [Dataset]. ScholarSphere.
description: Two samples of men were part of this study to receive either intravenous (IV) or intragastric (IG) infusions. All received 3 conditions: pure fat, pure carbohydrate, or isotonic saline in the morning. They consumed lunch ~30 min post infusion and dinner 6 hours post infusion. Participants rated hunger, thirst, fullness, prospective consumption, and nausea hourly. Blood was also drawn to asses physiological measurements for the IG group. Participants also completed a yogurt pre-load study with 3 conditions (each about 1 week apart) where they consumed mostly carbohydrate, mostly fat, or no yogurt preload before lunch.
